settings.heading: A Complete Timeline of Global Rug Styles and Trends
Evolution of rug styles over time

settings.text:
The evolution of rug styles demonstrates how ancient royal court traditions developed into contemporary 21st-century design. Each culture introduced its distinct weaving style to the Silk Road which resulted in area rugs transforming from essential tribal items into worldwide artistic creations.

1. Persian Rugs: The Gold Standard of Artistry Persian rugs which originated in present-day Iran stand as the most complex weaving achievement. The Safavid Dynasty (1501–1736) period
saw rug production transform from an itinerant handicraft into a government-operated manufacturing sector.

The Medallion Style: Most Persian living room rugs feature a central medallion, which symbolizes the "eye of God"2 or a lotus flower, and is surrounded by decorative floral vine scrolls known as islimi.

Royalty custom ordered these rugs which were created using high-knot-count silk and fine "kurk" wool. The "painting-like" design becomes more elaborate through increased knots per square inch.

2. Oriental Rugs: A Tapestry of the East The term "Persian" specifically identifies rugs which originate from Iran. The
term "Oriental" serves as a broader designation which includes rugs that originate from Turkey China India and the Caucasus regions.

The "Ghiordes" double knot serves as the main identification feature which defines Turkish Anatolian rugs. The rugs show their design identity through their use of strong geometric patterns which contrast with the smooth curves found in Persian design.

3. Chinese Rugs: The historical development of Chinese rugs started with their adoption of high-relief carving techniques which enabled them to create dragon and cloud and crane patterns.

The Indian Influence: India established itself as the first country to create textile products through plant fiber-based materials. The Indian textile industry produced high quality wool carpets while its jute rug production established the industry standard. Jute emerged as the superior choice for Southeast Asian humid conditions because it provided an economical and breathable and long-lasting alternative to heavy wool fabrics.

4. The period from 1900 to 2100 saw people abandon elaborate traditional designs in favour of basic functional designs and manufacturing progress.

Mid-Century Modern: The "shag" rug and geometric "Pop Art" rugs became popular, moving away from floral borders to abstract shapes and solid colours.

Round Rugs for Modern Layouts: Architects used round rugs to create visual discontinuity which softened their designs of compact residential spaces and wide-open industrial-style apartments.

5. The Rise of Washable Rugs: The most important change in modern times involves the development of rugs which can be washed. The rugs use advanced synthetic fibers which include recycled polyester to create a Persian antique appearance that can withstand home washing machine cleaning—a capability which historic wool textiles lack.
